transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. How can I help you today?

Well, hi. Thank you. I, um... I came in because I keep having these evenings where I just lose control. I'll stop and buy a whole family-size takeout order, and then I'll add on bags of chips or bakery things from the store, and I end up eating almost all of it myself before I even seem to register how much is gone. It's just... I don't know. 

I actually used to work at a bakery, years ago, right after I got my associate's degree. We made these incredible lemon bars. My supervisor back then, Brenda, she used to let us take the broken ones home. Brenda was a piece of work, though. She used to make us scrub the display cases twice a day, even if nobody had even leaned on them. Anyway, I supervise an office now, so I guess I understand why she was so strict about the little things, but still. What was I saying? Oh, right, the food. Yeah, I just... I eat so much of it before I even realize what I'm doing.
Can you describe what you mean by 'losing control' during these eating episodes? Do you feel unable to stop eating even if you want to?

Well, yes, exactly. It's like... once I start, there's this awful switch that just flips. I can literally be sitting there thinking, *Taylor, put it away, you don't need this*, but my hands just keep opening containers. It's like I'm not even the one in charge anymore. My ex-husband used to say I was a control freak—which, honestly, is rich coming from a man who insisted on organizing his sock drawer by thread count. I mean, who even does that? He'd spend hours on a Sunday just folding and refolding them while I was trying to get the house cleaned. Sundays were always my cleaning days because during the week, the office is just a madhouse. We had this new software update last Tuesday and half the staff couldn't even log in, so I spent three hours on the phone with IT. But, um... wait, what was the question? Oh, the eating. Right. Yeah, my hands just keep moving and I can't seem to make them stop, no matter what my brain is screaming at me.
After these eating episodes, do you feel guilty, ashamed, or upset with yourself about what you've eaten or how much you've eaten?

Guilty? Um... I'm not really sure, to be honest. I haven't really noticed feeling like that. Usually, I just feel incredibly exhausted right after. Speaking of exhausted, my commute has been an absolute nightmare lately. They're doing all this construction on the overpass near the office, and yesterday I sat in traffic for forty-five minutes just listening to the radio. They play the exact same five songs over and over on that morning show. I used to love listening to morning radio back in the nineties, though. They had those funny prank calls, you know? My sister and I used to record them on cassette tapes. She lives down in Florida now, so we don't talk as much, but she just got a new puppy. A golden retriever. They chew on absolutely everything, so I told her she better watch her good shoes. She loves buying expensive shoes, she has this whole closet just for heels. But, um... wait, what did you ask me? Something about after I eat? Yeah, I don't really know about feeling ashamed or upset or anything. I just haven't really paid attention to that.
After these eating episodes, do you ever make yourself sick, exercise excessively, or skip meals to try to control your weight or get rid of the calories you consumed?

Make myself sick? Oh, no. No, I don't do any of that. I definitely don't exercise, that's for sure. I used to, though! Back when I was in my thirties, I took this step aerobics class twice a week. It was so much fun, we all wore those bright leotards and the instructor, Gary, he was just hilarious. He had this huge mustache, like Tom Selleck. Do you remember Magnum P.I.? I used to watch that show with my dad all the time when I was growing up. We had this big, clunky TV with the dials you actually had to get up and turn. My dad always made me be the remote control. He'd say, "Taylor, turn it to channel 4," and I'd have to run over and click it. He was a good guy, my dad. He worked at the post office for thirty-five years. Always wore those little blue shorts in the summer, even when his legs were practically see-through. But, um... what were we talking about? Oh, right, skipping meals and stuff. No, I don't really do anything like that to get rid of the calories. I just... I just kind of go to bed or sit there feeling stuffed.
Do these eating episodes cause you significant distress or interfere with your daily life, like at work or with other activities?

Well, yes, they do. I mean, I've actually stopped inviting people over to the house. I used to love hosting, you know? I had this beautiful patio set I bought at Pier 1 before they closed all their stores. It was wrought iron with these lovely floral cushions. I spent a fortune on it, and now it just sits there. I used to have the girls from the office over for margaritas on Fridays, but now I just... I don't want anyone around. And I've been skipping my evening routines, too. Like, I used to do a little yoga in the living room, or go out and do my gardening chores. I had the most gorgeous hydrangeas last year, huge blue blooms. The secret is adding coffee grounds to the soil, it changes the acidity. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable, taught me that. She's been living next door since 1998, always wearing these enormous sun hats. But lately, I haven't even been out to water them. I just feel so ashamed and... preoccupied after I eat like that. It's like I can't focus on anything else, so I just hide away instead of doing the things I usually do.
How often do these episodes where you feel like you lose control while eating typically happen?

Well, I actually started keeping a journal about it. My niece got me this beautiful leather-bound one for Christmas. She's so thoughtful, she always finds the best gifts. She works at this boutique downtown, the one with the pink awning? They sell those fancy candles that smell like, I don't know, sandalwood and sea salt. I usually hate strong smells, they give me terrible headaches. I used to get migraines all the time when I was working at the bank back in my twenties. The fluorescent lights in that place were just awful, always buzzing. I don't know how anyone gets any work done with that constant hum. Anyway, the journal... right. So I've been writing things down, and when I look back through it, there has barely been a week in the last several months without at least one of these nights. Honestly, most weeks it happens several times. I'll just be sitting there, and before I know it... well, it's just happening a lot.
Do these eating episodes usually happen when you're not really hungry, or do they tend to happen when you're already feeling hungry?

Well, a lot of the time I'm not actually hungry at all. I mean, I might have just had a perfectly normal dinner. I usually make something simple, like baked chicken or a nice salad. I used to make these elaborate casseroles back when my husband was still around, he loved my tuna noodle casserole. I always added a little bit of crushed potato chips on top for a crunch, you know? That was a trick my mother taught me. She was a wonderful cook, could make a meal out of practically nothing. She grew up during the Depression, so she learned how to stretch a dollar. She used to save bacon grease in this little tin can on the stove... oh, I haven't thought about that tin can in years. It had a little picture of a farm on it. Anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, being hungry. So, I'll have dinner, and I'm full, but then later I just... I find myself looking through the fridge or the pantry shelves. It's almost like the food is just something I have to finish, even though my stomach isn't rumbling or anything.
During these episodes, do you find yourself eating much more rapidly than normal?

Yes, I do. It's... it's actually a blur. I eat so fast during those times that I barely taste anything. I'll just be standing there at the dining room table—it's this gorgeous oak table I found at an estate sale years ago. The woman who owned it was moving into an assisted living facility, and her daughter was just trying to clear out the house. I felt a little bad negotiating the price, but it was just so heavy, I had to pay my nephew and his friend to help me move it. My nephew, Jimmy, he's in his second year of college now, studying engineering. He's always been so smart, building little models out of toothpicks when he was just a boy. Anyway, I'll be standing at that table, and I'll have the microwave going, and empty boxes all around me. It's like I'm swallowing one bite while I'm already reaching for the next. I don't even sit down, I just eat as fast as I can.
Do you usually eat these large amounts of food in secret, like when you're alone or no one else is around?

Oh, absolutely. I could never... I make a point of doing it when my husband is asleep. Or, well, lately I have to wait until the contractors are gone. We're having the master bathroom redone, finally. It's been on the to-do list for a decade. The dust, though, it gets absolutely everywhere, no matter how much plastic sheeting they tape up over the doors. And the head contractor, Gary, he's nice enough, but he will talk your ear off about his golf swing. I don't know the first thing about golf. My father used to play, he had this heavy leather bag of clubs he kept polished in the garage, but I'm paying Gary to lay subway tile, not give me a sports commentary, you know? 

But anyway... what were we saying? Right, eating in secret. Yes, I wait until Gary and his crew pack up their trucks and my husband is snoring upstairs. I would just be absolutely mortified for anyone to see the sheer amount of food I can put away. Especially after acting so perfectly controlled all day at work. I supervise the whole administrative pool at my office, so I have to be the one who has everything together and keeps everyone in line. To go from that to... well, whatever I am at night, it's just too shameful. I have to be alone.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets diagnostic criteria for binge-eating disorder, including recurrent episodes of eating significantly more rapidly than normal, until feeling uncomfortably full, and despite not being physically hungry, eating alone due to embarrassment, and experiencing shame and functional impairment. There is no evidence of compensatory behaviors (e.g., purging, excessive exercise), distinguishing it from bulimia nervosa. The absence of significant distress about the behavior is atypical but does not exclude the diagnosis when functional impairment is present.
